title: Traffic leaves through a tor-pool exit
proves: The pool is wired end to end: the session key becomes the SOCKS username, the credential authenticates, and the egress IP is a Tor exit.

title: A session stays pinned to one exit across requests
proves: Stickiness is what makes a clearance reusable and lets per-zone history accrue. A rotating address would invalidate both.

steps.what: all four requests left from one exit

title: Rotating moves the session to a different exit
proves: Rotation is a reassignment inside the pool: the endpoint URL is unchanged, but the address behind it — and therefore the identity — is not.

title: A failure report reaches the pool with the kind derived from the layer
proves: This is the only signal that catches a soft block — a proxy relaying bytes cannot see a 403 or a captcha inside an HTTPS tunnel — and the pool weighs a report by its kind.

steps.what: the pool's health score moved for exactly one instance
it was weighed as a captcha

title: Rotating between published ranges is refused, against live pool state
proves: THE headline rule. Every Tor exit is on the same published lists, so a reputation block cannot be fixed by another one — and the decision is driven by what the running pool actually offers, not by a hardcoded assumption.

steps.what: a Tor pool clears nothing at layer 1
and names the address kind as the constraint
steps.value: no configured exit clears the reputation layer — datacenter and Tor ranges are published, so rotating between them cannot help. A residential or mobile-carrier exit is the only thing that moves this layer
